series.name: Adaalat 2.0
series.tagline: Everyone knows who did it. Can you PROVE it?
series.concept: Realistic criminal cases where everyone knows who's guilty — but proving it is the real challenge. Each episode is a carousel reel that walks the audience through a case, builds an evidence board, and challenges them to figure out what's missing before revealing the answer.

episodes.title: The Collapsed Building

slides.text: June 14th. 3 AM. A 6-storey building in Malad collapses during monsoon rain. 22 dead. 40 rescued. The builder goes on TV — says act of God, unprecedented rainfall. But the building next door? Not a scratch.

Green Valley Residency. 6 floors. 48 flats. Sold out in 3 months. Builder: Pramod Gaikwad — first-time developer, no track record. BMC approved the plan. OC issued 9 months ago. Families moved in, painted walls, set up kitchens. Then the building killed them.

Approved plan said 4 floors. Gaikwad built 6. Two extra floors, no revised approval. Foundation designed for 4, carrying 6. Steel rods thinner than required. Residents complained about wall cracks within 3 months. Wrote to BMC. Nobody came.

Gaikwad's lawyer: BMC approved it, OC proves it was safe, rainfall was 300% above normal. Natural disaster, not negligence. BMC points at Gaikwad. Gaikwad points at BMC. Everyone points at the rain. 22 families plan funerals.
The builder blames the rain. BMC blames the builder. Nobody's going to jail. You're the investigator. What's the one thing that can't be blamed on the weather?

The rubble talks. Concrete core samples show exact cement-to-sand ratio. Steel bars have grade markings — if plan says Fe 500 and rubble has Fe 415, that's fraud. Purchase invoices show what Gaikwad actually bought vs what was required. The BMC officer's bank got ₹15 lakh the week the OC was issued — from Gaikwad's cousin's company. That's not rain. That's murder.

episodes.synopsis: A newly constructed 6-storey apartment building collapses during the first monsoon, killing 22 residents. The builder says it was unprecedented rainfall. But every other building on the street is still standing.
episodes.caption: A building collapses. 22 people die. Builder says it was the rain. But concrete doesn't lie, steel doesn't forget, and bank statements don't care about the weather. What would YOU check first — the rubble or the money trail? #Adaalat2 #Case011

episodes.title: The Killer Surgeon

slides.text: Seven people walked into City Life Hospital for routine surgeries — gallbladder, hernia, appendix. None walked out. All died on Dr. Vivek Nair's table. His death rate is 4x the national average. The hospital just gave him a promotion.

Dr. Vivek Nair. 42. Senior surgeon, City Life Hospital, Lucknow. Fully qualified on paper. Hospital: 200 beds, Kapoor Medical Group. Seven patients — routine surgeries, all dead. Same pattern every time: dead patient, paperwork filed, family consoled, move on.

Three families asked for surgery videos. Hospital said OT cameras were 'not functioning' — every time. A nurse reported smelling alcohol on Nair twice before surgeries. Nothing happened. His promotion? He brings in ₹3 crore/year in surgical fees. Dead patients are a cost of business.

Nair's lawyer: complications happen. Consent forms say 'risk of death.' OT cameras? Technical issues. Alcohol claim? Unverified gossip from a disgruntled employee. The families aren't doctors — they can't prove what went wrong inside that OR.
Cameras off. Hospital protecting him. Consent forms cover everything. How do you prove a surgeon killed his patients when the hospital controls all the evidence?

Anaesthesia machines log everything — heartbeat, oxygen, drugs, timestamps. Hospital can't turn them off. Blood samples show dosage errors from a drunk doctor. Subpoena all four surgeons' records — if the other three are normal and Nair is 4x higher, that's a pattern. IT maintenance logs will show if cameras 'broke' only during Nair's surgeries.

episodes.synopsis: Seven patients die during routine surgeries at a private hospital over 18 months. All under one doctor — Dr. Vivek Nair. The hospital calls them unfortunate complications. The families smell something worse.
episodes.caption: Seven patients go in for routine surgery. None come out alive. The hospital says 'complications happen.' But anaesthesia machines don't lie, and patterns don't happen by accident. If you were investigating, what would you check first — the machine logs or the doctor's blood? #Adaalat2 #Case012

episodes.title: The Serial Bride

slides.text: Reshma Kaur. Or Priya Verma. Or Sana Malik. Or Neha Reddy. Four names, four marriages, four cities. In three years, she married four men through matrimonial apps. First three lost money. The fourth — Manpreet Singh — lost his life.
Husband 1: Deepak, Jaipur — Shaadi.com — ₹12 lakh gone. Husband 2: Farhan, Indore — Jeevansathi — ₹18 lakh. Husband 3: Venkat, Hyderabad — Bharatmatrimony — ₹22 lakh. Running total: ₹52 lakh stolen.

Husband 4: Manpreet Singh, Chandigarh. Real name this time. Family introduction. ₹1.2 crore life insurance — Reshma is nominee. Manpreet 'fell' from the terrace. ₹28 lakh already missing from his FDs — transferred two weeks before he died.

First three husbands never filed FIRs — too embarrassed. No official crime pattern. Reshma picks men who won't talk. Manpreet's death filed as accidental. She was 'inside the flat.' No eyewitness. No CCTV on the terrace.
Four identities. Three silent victims. One dead husband. She's about to collect ₹1.2 crore insurance. How do you stop her when none of her previous victims will even talk?

Aadhaar biometrics — one face, one fingerprint set across four names. Matrimonial apps store phone numbers and IP addresses. UPI transfers need KYC — follow the money trail. Manpreet's phone shows last 48 hours. Building entrance camera shows who was home that night. If only two people were there, she was on that terrace.

episodes.synopsis: Reshma Kaur has married four men across four states in three years using different names. Each husband discovered large sums missing after she vanished. The fourth husband is now dead — and his family says it wasn't an accident.
episodes.caption: She married four men in four cities with four names. Three lost their money. One lost his life. She's about to collect ₹1.2 crore insurance. But Aadhaar has one face, UPI has one trail, and apps remember every login. What would you trace first — the money or the identity? #Adaalat2 #Case013

episodes.title: The Poison on Your Plate

slides.text: Patna. Two weeks. 12 dead. 43 hospitalized. All consumed Shudh Gold mustard oil. Symptoms: vomiting, paralysis, swelling. Company owner blames the retailer. But deaths from 6 different shops in 6 neighborhoods. That's not storage. That's the source.

Shudh Gold — manufactured in Hajipur. Rajiv Agarwal took over two years ago. Expanded production, cut prices — suddenly the cheapest mustard oil in Bihar at ₹140/litre vs ₹210 for competitors. 12 dead across all neighborhoods. Only common link: the yellow bottle.

Shudh Gold was mixing argemone seed oil into mustard oil. Argemone looks like mustard seed — costs ₹20/kg vs ₹80. 30% mixed into every batch. Causes epidemic dropsy — swelling, paralysis, death. Two workers quit. FSSAI gave it a clean certificate 6 months ago.

FSSAI certificate says factory was approved. No lab report from actual killer bottles — families threw them away. Rajiv says argemone supplier mixed it without his knowledge. Supplier is a small farmer — cash payments only, no paper trail.
12 dead from poison oil. Bottles gone. Supplier is a ghost. Factory has a clean certificate. How do you prove the owner knew he was selling poison?

GST invoices show ₹20/kg from Rajasthan — real mustard costs ₹80. That price proves he knew. Seize unsold stock from shops and factory. Find the two workers who quit — bank accounts show salary. Check if FSSAI lab actually received a sample — if not, inspector faked it. Check the inspector's bank account.

episodes.synopsis: Twelve people die across Patna after consuming mustard oil from a single brand over two weeks. The company says it's a storage issue at the retailer's end. But the deaths span six different shops.
episodes.caption: Twelve people dead from mustard oil they used every day. The company says blame the shop. But ₹20-per-kilo 'mustard seed' from Rajasthan isn't mustard — and GST invoices don't lie. Would you check the factory's purchases first or the FSSAI inspector's bank account? #Adaalat2 #Case014

episodes.title: The Ransom Call

slides.text: Pune. A man in a helmet boards a school bus at a red light, takes 6-year-old Aarav by the hand. No weapon, no threat. Aarav goes willingly. 40 minutes later — ransom call for ₹50 lakh. From a number registered to Aarav's father. Who is sitting in the police station.

Sanjay Mehta — pharma distribution, ₹8 crore turnover. Wife at kitty party. ₹50 lakh would require liquidating assets. School bus: GPS-tracked, 8 CCTV cameras. Bus stopped 90 seconds at the signal. Man walked on, took child, walked off. Nobody stopped him.

Sanjay has 3 phone numbers. Third one — registered on Aadhaar — he says he 'lost' 6 months ago. Never reported to telecom. That SIM made the ransom call. Bus CCTV: Aarav recognized the man, extended his hand. Drop location: a specific dhaba on Pune-Mumbai Expressway. The kidnapper knows the area.

Two theories: father staged it, or someone framed him. Sanjay's alibi is airtight — office confirmed, car GPS confirmed. But the SIM is his, the kidnapper knew the child, the ransom matches his finances. Everything points to the father, but the father was somewhere else.
The SIM is the father's. The child went willingly. The ransom fits the bank balance. But the father has an airtight alibi. Who took the boy?

Aarav went willingly — check family photos for who he calls 'uncle.' The lost SIM was recharged after Sanjay lost it — UPI shows who paid. Dhaba drop: check Google/Zomato reviews for Sanjay's contacts. Brother Nitin fits: medium build, Aarav's uncle, ₹35 lakh debt to Sanjay. Check Nitin's phone location at 2:45 PM.

episodes.synopsis: Six-year-old Aarav Mehta is snatched from his school bus in Pune. The ransom demand of ₹50 lakh comes from a phone registered to his own father, who is at the police station when the call is made.
episodes.caption: A 6-year-old kidnapped from a school bus. Ransom demand from his own father's phone number. But the father is sitting in the police station. The boy didn't cry, the SIM was 'lost' six months ago, and the drop location is a dhaba someone in the family knows well. Who would you investigate first — the father or the uncle? #Adaalat2 #Case015

episodes.title: The Maid's Network

slides.text: Defence Colony, South Delhi. 4 months. 3 families. ₹40 lakh in gold — gone piece by piece. Guptas: ₹18 lakh. Bhallas: ₹12 lakh. Khannas: ₹10 lakh. All maids from one agency — Sewa Domestic Solutions. Three maids, three houses, same agency, same pattern.

Agency owner: Harish Taneja, 8 years in business. Maids: Pushpa, Sunita, Rekha — Aadhaar verified, police verified, no criminal records. Bank accounts show regular ₹8-12K transfers home. No suspicious deposits. Clean records, clean accounts. So where's the gold?

Thefts happen when families are home — from unlocked spots. Nanny cam: Pushpa never touches jewellery. Yet another piece vanished. Colony CCTV: all three maids leave through the same gate between 7 and 7:30 PM every evening.

Fingerprints irrelevant — they clean the house. Nanny cam shows nothing. Banks clean. Police searched their shared room — empty. Taneja: 8 years, zero complaints. No proof against anyone. ₹40 lakh vanished into thin air.
Three maids. Three families. ₹40 lakh in gold. No camera evidence, no bank trail, no jewellery found. How is gold disappearing without a trace?

Colony gate CCTV: who's WAITING outside at 7 PM? A man on a scooter every day — the collection agent. Handoff outside the gate. Trace the scooter to Taneja. Post in colony WhatsApp for more victims. Gold buyers within 5 km need PAN for purchases — check if Taneja's ID shows up.

episodes.synopsis: Three families in a posh South Delhi colony discover jewellery worth ₹40 lakh missing over four months. All three employ domestic help from the same placement agency. The maids deny everything.
episodes.caption: ₹40 lakh in gold vanishes from three houses. Nanny cams show nothing. Bank accounts are clean. But someone waits on a scooter outside the colony gate every evening at 7 PM — and old gold needs a PAN card to sell. Would you check the gate CCTV or the local jewellers first? #Adaalat2 #Case016

episodes.title: The Profile That Vanished

slides.text: Bangalore. Koramangala. Meera Kulkarni, 28, software engineer. Found strangled. No forced entry. Phone missing. Bumble conversation deleted. She'd been seeing 'Arjun' — three dates. Profile deleted. Person vanished.

Flatmate in Goa Friday-Sunday. Meera last seen alive Saturday. Zomato order for two at 8:15 PM. Two plates in sink. Instagram story 7:30 PM — two wine glasses, no face. Friends' description of Arjun: tall, beard, white car, consulting. That's all anyone knows.

No unidentified fingerprints — gloves or wiped down. 4th floor camera broken for 2 months. Lobby: tall man in cap and mask, 7:45 PM. No face. No visitor register — guard on chai break. Leaves 11:30 PM. Meera's phone — gone. He took it.

The killer planned everything: deleted profile, took phone, wore mask, chose night flatmate was away, broken camera on her floor. Bumble needs a court order. Police have no face, no name, no number. 'Tall, beard, white car' matches half of Koramangala.
No face. No name. No phone. Dating profile gone. Lobby camera useless. He planned everything. What did he forget?

Zomato delivery person came to the door — eyewitness. White car in parking lot — entry cameras log plates. WhatsApp backups on Meera's Google Drive may have his details. Bumble's server still has the phone number from his deleted account. He can delete his face. He can't delete his SIM registration.

episodes.synopsis: 28-year-old Meera Kulkarni is found dead in her Bangalore apartment three days after her last date with a man she met on Bumble. The dating profile has been deleted. No one knows his real name.
episodes.caption: She met him on Bumble. Three dates later, she's dead. He deleted his profile, took her phone, wore a mask. But Zomato's delivery guy saw him, the parking lot camera caught his car, and Bumble's server still has his phone number. What would you check first — the parking lot or her Google Drive backup? #Adaalat2 #Case017

episodes.title: The Kota Deathtrap

slides.text: Kota. 80 students in a basement classroom. Electrical fire. One staircase, one exit, no extinguishers, no ventilation. 14 students suffocate. The owner shows 5 fire safety certificates. All valid. The building that killed 14 children was officially safe.

Pinnacle IIT Academy. Owner: Suresh Rathore, failed engineering aspirant. 400 students, ₹2 crore/year. Basement — sealed windows for soundproofing. 80 chairs, zero fire exits. Students paid ₹1.5 lakh/year. Parents from small towns trusted the certificates on the wall.

5 certificates, all signed by one officer: B.L. Meena. One per year. Students: no fire drill ever. No extinguisher. Emergency exit sign painted on the wall — not a real exit. Meena approved 23 coaching centers last year. Same signature on all.
Rathore's lawyer: electrical accident, act of God. Certificates prove compliance. Meena says he inspected personally. Parents can't afford lawyers. Coaching lobby pushing for accident classification.
14 children dead in a basement with one exit. Owner has certificates. Fire officer says he inspected. How do you prove a government certificate is a lie?

Meena's Google Maps timeline for certificate dates — if his phone wasn't at the building, he never inspected. He approved 3 buildings on the same day in different areas — impossible. Check his family's bank accounts for deposits matching certificate dates. Sealed windows and no extinguishers are visible violations — the building itself proves he's lying.

episodes.synopsis: A fire breaks out at a basement coaching center in Kota, trapping 80 students. Fourteen die. The building had one exit, no fire extinguishers, and five fire safety certificates — all signed by the same officer.
episodes.caption: Fourteen students died in a basement with sealed windows and one exit. The owner had five fire certificates. But Google Maps knows where the inspector actually was, bank accounts know what he was paid, and sealed windows don't pass any inspection. Would you check the officer's phone or his bank account first? #Adaalat2 #Case018

episodes.title: The Fixed Innings

slides.text: Nagpur. Ranji Trophy quarterfinal. Star batsman Rohit Patil — season average 58 — scores 14 and gets out playing a wild slog against a spinner. Team loses by 11 runs. In the dressing room, his phone buzzes: PhonePe — ₹30,00,000 received.

Rohit Patil. Small-town Kolhapur. Father: schoolteacher. IPL scouts were watching — a good innings could mean ₹5-10 crore contract. Instead, 14 runs. The ₹30 lakh came from Desert Star Trading LLC, Dubai — shell company, no website, no employees. Money landed 11:47 PM the night before.

17 calls to an unsaved number that week — prepaid SIM, fake Aadhaar. Patil played 28 balls carefully, then suddenly a wild slog on ball 29. Coach: 'Never seen him play like that.' Dubai betting markets: ₹200 crore wagered on Vidarbha. Odds shifted 30 minutes before the match.

Patil's lawyer: bad day, every batsman has one. The ₹30 lakh? Wedding gift from a Dubai cousin. Phone calls? A friend. The shot? Cricket is unpredictable. BCCI needs proof of an agreement to fix — not just money and calls.
Star batsman scores 14 when he should score 80. ₹30 lakh from Dubai the night before. But bad days happen and wedding gifts exist. How do you prove a cricketer sold a match?

Wedding gift? Check if there's an actual wedding — venue bookings, caterers, invitations. Cousin earns ₹80K/month in Dubai — can't save ₹30 lakh. The fake SIM's phone has an IMEI — trace the buyer. Patil's WhatsApp Google Drive backup may have bookie chats. The PhonePe came through an Indian intermediary account — follow it to find who else was paid before other matches.

episodes.synopsis: In a crucial Ranji Trophy quarterfinal, star batsman Rohit Patil scores exactly 14 runs and gets out playing an inexplicable shot. His team loses by 11 runs. A ₹30 lakh PhonePe transfer from Dubai arrived the night before.
episodes.caption: Star batsman averages 58 all season, then scores 14 in the biggest match of his career. ₹30 lakh from Dubai lands the night before. He says it's a wedding gift. But there's no wedding, the cousin earns ₹80K a month, and the intermediary bank account has paid other players too. Would you check the PhonePe trail or the cousin's salary first? #Adaalat2 #Case019

episodes.title: The Ambulance Harvest

slides.text: Bhopal. Three accident victims, two months. All picked up by LifeLine Emergency ambulance. All declared dead on arrival. Families preparing funerals find surgical incisions — a kidney removed from each body. The ambulance owner? Dr. Ashok Tiwari. Who also runs a kidney transplant clinic.

Three victims: Ramesh (motorcycle accident), Priya (auto collision), Mohammad (truck hit). All conscious when loaded into the ambulance. All dead 35-40 minutes later. But 8 km should take 15 minutes max. Where did 25 minutes go?

Tiwari's clinic: New Life Kidney Center. 40 transplants in 2 years — government waitlist is 5 years, his patients get kidneys in weeks. The ambulance had a surgical setup inside — overhead light, instrument tray. Not standard. It was an operating table on wheels. If families had cremated, nobody would ever know.

Tiwari's lawyer: patients died from accident injuries. Post-mortem says head trauma. Missing kidneys? Maybe the hospital mortuary. Surgical setup? RTO approved for advanced life support. Transplants? All from voluntary donors with consent forms.

Three victims loaded alive, arrived dead. Kidneys removed in between. The ambulance has a surgical setup. The owner runs a transplant clinic. But post-mortem says accident injuries. How do you prove they were alive long enough for someone to take their kidneys?

Ambulance GPS shows exact route — if it stopped near Tiwari's clinic for 20 minutes, that's the crime scene. Bystanders saw victims conscious — phone videos exist. Cross-reference transplant dates with ambulance death dates. Transplant recipients got 'kidney available' calls on the same days. The timing will match.

episodes.synopsis: Three road accident victims in Bhopal are picked up by a private ambulance service. All three declared dead on arrival. All three missing a kidney. The ambulance owner also runs a transplant clinic.
episodes.caption: They got into the ambulance alive. They arrived at the hospital dead. Their kidneys were already gone. An 8 km ride took 40 minutes, and the GPS shows where the ambulance stopped. Would you check the GPS route or the transplant clinic's surgery dates first? #Adaalat2 #Case020

episodes.title: The University That Never Was

slides.text: Noida. 200 students attended NITM for 4 years — lectures, exams, convocation. Then employers said: degree not recognized by AICTE or UGC. Worth nothing. The founder Dr. K.K. Srivastava is missing. Phone off. Campus locked. ₹20 crore in fees — gone.

Professional setup: website, prospectus, fake placement brochure showing Infosys/TCS. Newspaper ads across UP and Bihar. Parents visited campus — saw classrooms, library, lab. Paid ₹2.5 lakh/year. Annual convocation with a retired judge as chief guest. Nobody checked if it was recognized.

Building rented, 10-year lease. Hired real retired professors — ₹30K/month. Real syllabi, real exams. Counterfeit marksheets with fake holograms. 7 years, 3 batches, 350+ victims. First two batches working with fake degrees. Third batch discovered the fraud.

Srivastava planned his exit — sold fixtures, emptied accounts, vanished 3 months ago. Bank account closed, money withdrawn in cash. Professors say they had no idea. Phone off, Aadhaar address vacated. 350 people's four years bought them nothing.
The man has vanished. Money is cash. Phone off. Building empty. How do you find someone who spent 7 years planning his disappearance?

He lived 7 years — utility bills, Swiggy orders don't stop overnight. Check his last payments for a new location. Newspaper job ads were paid for — trace that phone/account. Landlord has his PAN, Aadhaar from the lease. Security deposit refund went to a new account. Check immigration records. New phone recharges are traceable through payment method.

episodes.synopsis: Two hundred students who graduated from NITM in Noida discover their degrees are not recognized. The campus was real, classes were real, the degree is fake. The founder has vanished with ₹20 crore.
episodes.caption: 200 students spent 4 years in a university that doesn't exist. Real classes, real exams, fake degree. The founder vanished with ₹20 crore in cash. But utility bills don't stop, landlords keep lease documents, and phone recharges leave a trail. Would you track the landlord's records or the immigration database first? #Adaalat2 #Case021

episodes.title: The Dead Harvest

slides.text: Yavatmal, Maharashtra. 15 farmers spray CropShield Max on cotton fields. Within 72 hours, every plant is dead. 3 farmers take their lives. ₹3 crore crop loss. AgroVita Chemicals — ₹500 crore company — blames 'improper dilution by untrained farmers.' They blame the dead.

AgroVita Chemicals, Hyderabad. ₹500 crore revenue. CropShield Max: new this season, 'revolutionary,' ₹800/litre. Their field rep Vijay Deshmukh personally visited all 15 farmers. He demonstrated the mixing. He watched them spray. These farmers didn't guess from a label.

Label says Profenofos 40%. Informal test: actual concentration nearly 3x higher — kills plants, not pests. One farmer kept an unopened bottle. AgroVita priced 30% below competitors. To hit that price, quality had to give. The cheapness was the poison.

AgroVita has lawyers. Product passed CIB registration. Informal test isn't admissible. Farmers are 'illiterate, could have mixed wrong.' Field rep Deshmukh on sudden 'medical leave.' Three widows can't afford bus fare to court.
15 farmers trusted a company. 3 are dead. The label says one thing, the crops say another. How do you make a ₹500 crore company answer for dead farmers?

Send the unopened bottle to an accredited government lab — admissible in court. Buy more from shops with the same batch number. Deshmukh's phone has visit photos/videos — AgroVita's system has his reports. Subpoena factory batch records for quality checks. Check other talukas for same problems — post in Krishi Vigyan Kendra WhatsApp groups.

episodes.synopsis: Fifteen farmers in Yavatmal lose their cotton crop after using a new pesticide. Three farmers commit suicide. The company says improper application. But their own field rep demonstrated the mixing.
episodes.caption: A pesticide company sells poison labeled as protection. 15 farmers' crops die. 3 farmers die. The company blames the farmers. But one kept an unopened bottle, the field rep documented his own demonstrations, and factory batch records don't lie. Would you test the spare bottle or subpoena the factory records first? #Adaalat2 #Case022

episodes.title: The Stolen Signature

slides.text: Lucknow. A 78-year-old in a torn kurta found on the Kanpur highway at 2 AM. Harish Chandra Mishra — retired professor. His ₹4 crore house and plot registered to his son Rakesh three weeks ago. Gift deed — signed, witnessed, registered. Father says he doesn't remember signing anything.

Mishra: widower, retired 15 years. Rakesh: garment business, ₹60 lakh in debt, loans from private moneylenders. The house and plot were the old man's only assets. Daughter Deepa visits monthly. Rakesh visited weekly — 'to check on Papa.'

Gift deed registered Feb 3rd — thumb impression, not signature. Witnesses: Rakesh's employee and neighbor. Sub-registrar says 'present and willing.' But Mishra has severe cataracts — nearly blind — and early dementia. Daughter was never informed.

Rakesh's lawyer: deed is legally registered, Aadhaar verified, thumb matches. 'Father has good days and bad days. Feb 3rd was a good day.' Sub-registrar: procedure followed. One old man's word against a registered government document.
A nearly blind man with dementia 'gifts' ₹4 crore to his debt-ridden son. Deed registered, thumb matches. How do you prove a legal document was obtained by fraud?

Sub-registrar's CCTV shows the registration — was Mishra alert or being guided? His phone GPS shows he was transported there and back. Doctor's records prove cognitive decline before Feb 3rd — legally incapable of consent. Rakesh took a loan against the property two weeks later and listed the plot on 99acres. That's not a gift — that's theft with paperwork.

episodes.synopsis: 78-year-old retired professor Harish Chandra Mishra is found on a Lucknow highway. His ₹4 crore property has been registered to his son via a gift deed. The father says he was drugged and thrown out.
episodes.caption: A 78-year-old man with dementia and near-blindness 'gifts' his ₹4 crore property to his debt-ridden son. The deed is registered, the thumb print matches, and the government stamp is real. But the sub-registrar has CCTV, the doctor has records, and 99acres has the plot already listed for sale. Would you check the registration video or the medical records first? #Adaalat2 #Case023

episodes.title: The Wedding Feast

slides.text: Jaipur. The Grand Meridian — 5-star. Wedding dinner for 500 guests. By midnight, 80 in the ER. By morning, 2 elderly guests dead. Both ate the paneer tikka and malai kofta. Hotel GM on damage control. Caterer issuing statements. Nobody accepting blame.

Hotel provided kitchen, cold storage, serving staff. Royal Rasoi caterer brought chefs and raw materials. 22 dishes — hospital reports point to paneer tikka and malai kofta. Paneer supplied by caterer but stored in hotel's cold storage for 14 hours before cooking.

Cold storage should be 4°C for dairy. Temperature logs for Dec 17th — the day paneer was stored — are deleted. Hotel says 'system glitch.' Caterer delivered fresh paneer at 6 AM. 14 hours in hotel storage. No temperature check before cooking — FSSAI requires it.

Hotel: caterer supplied bad paneer. Caterer: hotel storage was broken, that's why they deleted logs. Hotel maintenance: 8 months overdue. Caterer's supplier: no cold chain docs. The deleted log is the key evidence. Without it — he said, she said.
2 dead from a wedding dinner. The cold storage log was deleted. Hotel says glitch, caterer says cover-up. How do you prove the temperature when the data is gone?

Commercial cold rooms have a physical SD card recorder — IT can't delete hardware. If SD card is missing, that's tampering. Check all 12 hotels' maintenance — this one overdue = pattern of neglect. Kitchen staff WhatsApp groups know when it was warm. Map which guests ate what vs who got sick — isolates contamination to paneer dishes.

episodes.synopsis: 80 guests hospitalized and two die after a wedding dinner at a 5-star Jaipur hotel. Hotel blames the caterer. Caterer blames the hotel's cold storage. Someone deleted the kitchen temperature records.
episodes.caption: 500 guests at a 5-star wedding dinner. 80 get sick. 2 die. The cold storage temperature log was 'accidentally' deleted. But the hardware recorder has an SD card, the kitchen staff have a WhatsApp group, and 420 healthy guests prove which dishes were the poison. Would you check the SD card or interview the kitchen staff first? #Adaalat2 #Case024

episodes.title: The 2 AM Hit

slides.text: Mumbai. Marine Drive. 2:17 AM. White Range Rover at 110 km/h kills a woman and her two children sleeping on the pavement. Actor Karan Sehgal in the back seat. Driver Raju says he was driving. Blood alcohol tested 9 hours later — conveniently clean.

Karan Sehgal. A-list, ₹200 crore net worth. Club CCTV: drinking until 1:30 AM, couldn't walk. Friends helped him to his car at 1:45 AM. Driver Raju: ₹25K/month, 11 years service. The officer took 9 hours to test blood alcohol — same officer seen at Karan's parties.

Range Rover has 6 airbags — only driver-side deployed. Raju has bruised chest from airbag. But driver's seat pushed all the way back — Raju is 5'4", Karan is 6'1". Karan has forehead bruise and hand abrasions — steering wheel injuries, not sleeping-in-back injuries.

Karan's top lawyer files bail in hours. Raju confessed — signed statement. Blood test negative. Seat? 'Raju adjusts it sometimes.' Injuries? 'Hit the back of the front seat.' Raju promised his family will be 'taken care of.' ₹25K driver taking the fall for a ₹200 crore actor.
The driver confessed. Blood test negative. Lawyer says Karan was sleeping. 3 people dead and the killer is about to walk. How do you put the actor behind the wheel?

Club parking CCTV shows which door friends put Karan in. The car's ECU logged the driver's weight at impact — 85 kg (Karan) vs 58 kg (Raju). Raju's phone location data shows it was in the back seat. The Sea Link has cameras that photograph every car — at 2 AM, the driver's face is visible through the windshield.

episodes.synopsis: Bollywood actor Karan Sehgal's Range Rover kills three pavement dwellers on Marine Drive at 2 AM. His driver claims he was driving. But the seat position, airbag sensor, and Sea Link cameras tell a different story.
episodes.caption: A Bollywood star's Range Rover kills 3 people at 2 AM. His driver says he was driving. But the car seat was set for a 6'1" man, the airbag sensor recorded 85 kg, and the Sea Link camera photographed the driver's face through the windshield. Would you check the club CCTV or the car's computer first? #Adaalat2 #Case025

episodes.title: The Chit Fund King

slides.text: Bardhaman, West Bengal. Sonar Bangla Savings. 5 years. 12,000 depositors — rickshaw pullers, tea sellers, teachers. ₹400 crore collected. 30% returns promised. Jan 5th: office locked, phone off, staff gone. Anirban Mondal is at his Shantiniketan farmhouse sipping tea.

Scheme: ₹1,000/month deposits, ₹15,600/year return — 30%. Classic Ponzi — new deposits paying old investors. Not registered with SEBI, RBI, or ROC. Pink handwritten receipts, no serial numbers. All cash. No bank account in the company name.

On paper: mud house, ₹3 lakh income. Reality: Shantiniketan farmhouse (wife's name), Kolkata flat (brother's name), Fortuner (shell company), boarding school ₹8 lakh/year. 35 agents across the district collected cash for 10% commission. The agents live next door to the victims.

Anticipatory bail filed. Lawyer: 'private savings club, not regulated, consenting adults.' Properties 'independently owned' by wife and brother. The office: one desk, one chair, blank receipts. No ledger, no computer, no records. ₹400 crore — no paper trail.
₹400 crore in cash. No bank records, no registration, no ledger. The office is empty. How do you trace money that was never digitized?

₹400 crore enters banking when properties are purchased — check registrar and dealer payment records. 35 agents earned 10% commission — check their bank accounts for sudden spending. 12,000 pink receipts with dates/amounts can be digitized. School fees paid by DD or transfer reveal source accounts.

episodes.synopsis: Anirban Mondal's Sonar Bangla Savings collected ₹400 crore from 12,000 daily wage workers promising 30% returns. Classic Ponzi. All cash, no records. He lives in a mud house on paper but owns a farmhouse, a flat, and a Fortuner.
episodes.caption: 12,000 people invested ₹400 crore in a savings club that promised 30% returns. All cash, no records, pink receipts. But farmhouses need registration, boarding schools need fee payments, and 35 agents who earned commissions now have bank accounts that talk. Would you trace the property payments or interrogate the agents first? #Adaalat2 #Case026

episodes.title: 3 Kilometers of Rage

slides.text: Ahmedabad. SG Highway. 11:40 PM. An auto makes a lane change. BMW X5 honks. What follows: 3 km, 4 signals. At Thaltej crossroad, the BMW rams the auto at full speed. Auto flips. Driver Hansraj Solanki, 52 — dead. BMW driver: Dhruv Parikh, 23. Family net worth: ₹300 crore.

Dhruv: 23, 2 prior traffic violations settled. At a lounge till 11:15 PM — Instagram story at 11:08 PM. BMW has dashcam — lawyer seized it, refuses to hand over. Claims 'private property.' Dhruv's story: 'Auto scratched my car. I followed to get his number. Accidentally rear-ended him.'

No skid marks from BMW at crash site — no braking before impact at 80+ km/h. Passenger Neha told first responder: 'The car was chasing us.' 4 traffic cameras on SG Highway. BMW ran at least 2 red lights during the chase.

Bail in 18 hours. Lawyer: road rage, not premeditated — not murder. Dashcam 'private property.' Neha in ICU, can't give formal statement. Auto destroyed. Investigating officer already transferred once.
BMW chased an auto for 3 km, rammed it at full speed. Driver says accident. Dashcam locked away. Witness in ICU. How do you prove a 3 km chase was intentional?

SG Highway's 4 traffic cameras captured the entire chase — public footage, not 'private property.' Lounge CCTV + credit card receipts show how much Dhruv drank. His phone's Google Maps shows speed spiking over 3 km. Crash-site photos from bystanders show no scratch on BMW sides — only front damage from ramming.

episodes.synopsis: A BMW X5 chases an auto-rickshaw for 3 km through Ahmedabad before ramming it. Auto driver dies. BMW driver — son of a ₹300 crore developer — says the auto scratched his car.
episodes.caption: A BMW chased an auto for 3 km through 4 traffic signals and rammed it at 80 km/h. No braking. The driver says it was an accident. But 4 traffic cameras filmed the entire chase, his Google Maps logged his speed, and crash-site photos show no scratch that started it. Would you pull the traffic camera footage or his Google Maps data first? #Adaalat2 #Case027

episodes.title: The Holy Heist

slides.text: Kumbakonam, Tamil Nadu. Murugan temple — 1,200 years old. 3,000 devotees daily. Official income: ₹3 crore/year. Estimated by footfall: ₹12 crore. ₹9 crore missing every year. Head priest Swami Venkatesh — 15 years in charge, drives a Mercedes, lives in a mansion. Explanation: 'Family wealth.'

Venkatesh controls day-to-day operations, supervises Tuesday hundi opening. Staff of 12 — all hired by him. Accountant: his nephew. Security guard: his driver's brother. It's a family operation in temple clothes.

Former employee says hundi boxes have false bottoms — cash falls through to hidden compartment, emptied at night by Venkatesh. Black bags into Mercedes boot. Gold donations registered vaguely — 'miscellaneous items.' 2 kg goes in, 800 gm comes out on the register.

Lawyer calls the ex-employee 'disgruntled.' Hundi: 'standard design.' Mercedes: 'family inheritance.' Trust members: 'We trust Venkatesh.' HR&CE last audit: 2017 — 6 years ago. Devotees donate anonymously. No receipts. How do you prove theft when donors don't know what they gave?
₹9 crore vanishes yearly from a temple. Donations anonymous. Counting controlled by one man. Hundi boxes might be rigged. How do you catch a thief inside a temple?

Inspect the hundi — if false bottom exists, it's physical evidence. Venkatesh's income tax: ₹15K/month salary vs ₹2.8 crore assets = unexplained wealth. CCTV footfall x average donation = mathematical proof of ₹12 crore. Plant marked currency with recorded serial numbers — trace where those notes end up.

episodes.synopsis: The Murugan temple in Kumbakonam collects an estimated ₹12 crore/year but only ₹3 crore appears in accounts. The head priest drives a Mercedes on a ₹15,000 salary. The hundi boxes have false bottoms.
episodes.caption: A temple collects ₹12 crore but only ₹3 crore reaches the books. The head priest drives a Mercedes on a ₹15,000 salary. The hundi boxes have false bottoms, and the man who counts the money hired his own family. Would you inspect the boxes or check the priest's tax returns first? #Adaalat2 #Case028

episodes.title: The Ghost Children

slides.text: Kolkata. Aashray Foundation — children's home since 2016. 200 orphans on paper. ₹48 lakh/year from government + ₹30 lakh in donations. Surprise inspection: 140 children. Register says 200. 60 children exist on paper, on Aadhaar, in school forms — but not in reality.

Madhumita Sen, 51. No child welfare background — knew how to write grants. Sole signatory on the bank account. NRI donations via Instagram — beautiful photos, heartwarming stories. Donors in US/UK never visited.

60 ghost children each have Aadhaar numbers and school enrollment. School attendance: near zero — Madhumita said they were 'frequently ill.' ₹14.4 lakh/year skimmed from government grants. Plus donations. Total fraud: ₹1.2 crore over 5 years.

Madhumita: '60 children were recently rehabilitated with families — register not updated.' School enrollment: 'school's responsibility.' Aadhaar: 'provided by families.' NRI donors never visited. ICPS last inspection: 3 years ago.
60 children on Aadhaar, on school rolls, in government records — but not in the real world. The founder says 'rehabilitated.' How do you prove children who are supposed to be orphans never existed?

Aadhaar links to biometrics — verify if 60 numbers have valid fingerprints/iris scans. If fabricated, no biometrics. JJB must approve any child leaving care — check for discharge orders. Instagram group photos: borrowed children for photo ops. NRI donation receipts saying 'for 200 children' are each a document of fraud — donors become witnesses.

episodes.synopsis: Aashray Foundation runs a children's home for 200 orphans. Government funds ₹2,000/child/month. A surprise inspection finds only 140. Sixty children on the register don't exist. But their Aadhaar numbers do.
episodes.caption: A children's home claims 200 orphans. Only 140 exist. 60 have Aadhaar numbers but no biometrics, school enrollment but no attendance, and government funding but no mouths to feed. The founder raised ₹1.2 crore for ghost children. Would you verify the Aadhaar biometrics or check the Juvenile Justice Board records first? #Adaalat2 #Case029

episodes.title: The Moneylender's Last Entry

slides.text: Varanasi. Pappu Yadav — loan shark. Found dead at 6 AM. Blunt force trauma with his own brass paperweight. ₹4 lakh cash untouched in the drawer. Not robbery — personal. 300 borrowers at 5% monthly interest. Half the colony wanted him dead.

All cash operation. Handwritten ledger. ₹2 crore in outstanding loans — uncollectable with Pappu dead. Debts die with the lender when there's no legal docs. 300 suspects who all benefit from his death.

After 11 PM, only way in is a side door with a smart lock — pay ₹1 via UPI to unlock for 30 seconds. Pappu tracked who came at night. Time of death: midnight to 2 AM. Three ₹1 payments that night — Chotu, Bablu, and one unknown prepaid wallet on a new SIM activated 2 days before.
The third UPI payment: prepaid wallet, new SIM activated 2 days before. Minimal KYC. The killer planned it — new SIM, new wallet, one payment. A disposable trail.
The killer paid ₹1 to unlock the door. Burner wallet, new SIM, bought 2 days ago. How do you find a killer who paid for entry with a disposable phone?

Trace the SIM activation shop — register may have buyer's face. Wallet top-up came from somewhere traceable. Ledger narrows 300 to 10 most desperate debtors. The killer carried their real phone too — cell tower data shows which personal phone was near the office at midnight. Cross-reference with the ledger's top debtors.

episodes.synopsis: Loan shark Pappu Yadav found dead in his Varanasi office. 300 borrowers, all with motive. The killer entered through a smart-lock door that requires a ₹1 UPI payment — and the payment trail leads somewhere.
episodes.caption: A loan shark is murdered in his office. 300 people wanted him dead. But the killer paid ₹1 UPI to unlock the door, used a burner SIM bought 2 days ago, and still carried their real phone. Cell towers don't forget, and ₹8 lakh in debt is a powerful motive. Would you trace the SIM shop or check the cell tower data first? #Adaalat2 #Case030

episodes.title: The River Knows

slides.text: Sidhi, Madhya Pradesh. Journalist Suresh Tiwari's car in the Son River. Dead. Police: 'accidental drowning.' But at 9:02 PM — 30 minutes before — Suresh posted a Facebook Live from an illegal sand mining site. Named the MLA: Raghu Singh Patel. 45,000 views. Suresh is dead.

Suresh: YouTube channel 'Sidhi Ki Awaaz,' 80K subscribers. Covered sand mining for 2 years. Sand mining: ₹50,000 crore industry. In Sidhi, it's Patel — MLA, officially a 'farmer,' controls 40 trucks, no permits. Police look away. Suresh was the only journalist who didn't.

Facebook Live: 7 minutes, named Patel 3 times. 'If something happens to me, this video is my testament.' Wife's call at 9:15 PM: 'Two trucks are following me.' Car's rear bumper: impact damage — not from the river. Like another vehicle pushed it.

Police filed accident in 48 hours. IO reports to SP who reports to district admin where Patel is MLA. Bumper damage: 'rocks in the river.' Facebook Live: 'irrelevant.' Wife's testimony: 'unverified.' FIR closed. Patel on TV: 'Saddened by the unfortunate accident.'
Journalist names the mafia boss on Facebook Live. 30 minutes later, car is in a river. Police: accident. MLA: unfortunate. How do you reopen a case the system already closed?

Suresh's Google Maps shows his speed — sudden stop means rammed, not drift. FASTag toll booth 2 km before the river logged every truck. Match truck plates from the Facebook Live video to the toll booth. Go above local police: CBI or High Court Article 226. Video = motive, toll = opportunity, bumper = method.

episodes.synopsis: Journalist Suresh Tiwari's car found in the Son River. Police say accident. But he posted a Facebook Live 30 minutes before his death exposing illegal sand mining and naming the MLA behind it.
episodes.caption: A journalist names the sand mafia boss on Facebook Live. 30 minutes later, he's dead in a river. Police call it an accident. But Google Maps shows his speed, FASTag shows which trucks were behind him, and 45,000 people watched the video that named his killer. Would you pull the toll records or the phone's GPS first? #Adaalat2 #Case031

episodes.title: The ATM Trap

slides.text: Chennai. T. Nagar. SBI ATM on Usman Road. One Saturday, 200 customers wake up to 'Amount debited' SMS. Transactions from ATMs in Delhi, Lucknow, Hyderabad — cities they've never visited. ₹40 lakh stolen in one weekend. All used the same ATM. It looks perfectly normal.

ATM skimming: device on card slot copies magnetic stripe, pinhole camera records PIN. Criminals make cloned cards, withdraw from other cities in one weekend. 3 weeks of data collection, then one weekend of mass withdrawals before banks detect it.

15 ATMs in 3 cities, simultaneous Saturday night withdrawals — at least 15 gang members. Last SBI inspection: 5 weeks ago. ATM booth CCTV tilted to show ceiling — moved when the regular guard went sick and a 'substitute' showed up for one shift. That substitute installed the skimmer.

SBI: 'Under investigation.' 200 individual FIRs needed. Skimmer removed — no physical evidence. CCTV aimed at ceiling. Substitute guard gave fake name and phone. The evidence walked away with the criminals.
200 robbed through a device that's gone. CCTV sabotaged. Substitute guard was a ghost. Money withdrawn in 3 cities simultaneously. How do you catch a gang that leaves no physical evidence?

The 15 withdrawal ATMs have working CCTV — gang members' faces are recorded. Usman Road has shop cameras — trace the substitute guard. The skimmer uses Bluetooth — nearby shop CCTV shows someone loitering daily with a phone. Withdrawal transactions match ATM camera timestamps — faces matched to cloned card uses.

episodes.synopsis: 200 Chennai customers lose ₹40 lakh after using one ATM. A skimming device harvested card data for 3 weeks. The CCTV was sabotaged. A substitute guard installed the skimmer.
episodes.caption: 200 people lose ₹40 lakh from one ATM in Chennai. The skimming device is gone. The CCTV was sabotaged. But the gang members withdrew cash from 15 ATMs in other cities — and those cameras worked fine. Would you pull the withdrawal ATM footage or trace the substitute guard on street cameras? #Adaalat2 #Case032

episodes.title: The Goldsmith's Secret

slides.text: Jaipur. Johari Bazaar. Kanhaiya Gold House — 3 generations, 60 years. Then customers came back: bangles turning green, chains discoloring. Gold doesn't tarnish. Unless it's not gold all the way through. 500+ customers. ₹15 crore. The owner says 'minor quality issue.'

The trick: tungsten core, gold coating. Tungsten density = gold density (19.3 vs 19.25 g/cm3). Weight matches. Acid test only touches the surface — passes. After 6 months, gold wears thin at stress points and tungsten shows through. The perfect fraud.

BIS hallmark certificates issued by local assayer Govind Sharma. He drilled into the gold surface — tested genuine — and stamped '22K 916.' Never drilled deep enough to hit tungsten. Purchase records: 200 kg gold bought. Sales: 350 kg 'gold' sold. Where did the extra 150 kg come from?

Kanhaiya's lawyer: supplier's fault, hallmark backs it up. Sharma: tested properly. BIS: can't guarantee everything. Many customers have no receipts — cash purchases. Acid test still shows gold on surface. The system that verifies gold verified the fraud.
Gold passes the acid test. Hallmark is real. Weight matches. But 500 customers have jewellery turning green. How do you prove gold is fake when every test says it's real?

Cut one bangle in half — cross-section shows tungsten core instantly. A hacksaw and 5 minutes. GST invoices: 200 kg bought vs 350 kg sold — the math doesn't work without tungsten. Kanhaiya bought tungsten somewhere — Amazon/IndiaMART track orders. Digital payments + billing software database = receipts for cash customers too.

episodes.synopsis: Jaipur's Kanhaiya Gold House sold gold-plated tungsten as 22-karat gold for 2 years. 500+ customers, ₹15 crore fraud. It passes the acid test. But six months later, it turns green.
episodes.caption: 60 years of trust. 500 cheated customers. ₹15 crore in gold-plated tungsten sold as 22-karat gold. It passed the acid test and the hallmark — but a hacksaw tells you the truth in 5 minutes, and GST invoices show 200 kg bought but 350 kg sold. Would you cut the bangle or pull the purchase records first? #Adaalat2 #Case033
